items.title: Federal judge denies Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron's motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing class action alleging supply restriction conspiracy [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Court denies motion to dismiss DRAM price fixing case
items.summary:
A federal judge in the Northern District of California denied a motion to dismiss a proposed class action accusing Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron of conspiring to restrict conventional DRAM supply, which allegedly led to significant price increases. The judge found the complaint plausibly alleged an agreement violating antitrust laws, distinguishing it from a previous dismissed case involving the same companies.

The suit, filed by consumers and small businesses from five states, claims the companies controlled over 91% of global DRAM revenue and coordinated production cuts starting in late 2022 while shifting capacity to high bandwidth memory (HBM). The court found several factors, including long-term HBM contracts and delayed plant expansions, supported the allegation of a conspiracy beyond lawful parallel conduct. The companies must respond by December 7, 2026, with the initial case management conference set for January 12, 2027.

items.title: Author argues for seriously considering ongoing rapid AI progress and its transformative societal impact beyond short-term AGI timelines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Taking AI Seriously
items.summary:
The article discusses the evolving perspectives on artificial intelligence in software engineering and society, emphasizing the importance of taking AI progress seriously rather than assuming it will plateau. It critiques common attitudes that underestimate AI's potential and calls for acknowledging the possibility that AI advancements will continue at a rapid pace, profoundly affecting various fields such as software, mathematics, and cybersecurity.

The author distinguishes between believing in imminent AGI timelines and recognizing AI's transformative consequences, advocating for a nuanced view that considers ongoing progress as a plausible scenario. Using a metaphor from Borges' story Tlön, the article illustrates how new realities can gradually reshape our world, suggesting that society should be open to the significant changes AI may bring rather than dismissing them prematurely.

items.title: Baltimore County Public Schools to phase out AI reading program Amira by next school year, citing parent feedback and screen time concerns [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Baltimore County schools phase out AI reading program
items.summary:
Baltimore County Public Schools announced it will discontinue the AI-powered reading program Amira for kindergarten to third-grade students by the next school year, allowing limited use only for struggling students and optional family access. The decision follows feedback from parents, staff, and administrators aiming to reduce screen time for young learners.

The program had previously been credited by the former superintendent for improving reading growth, but some parents expressed concerns about excessive screen use and its impact on children. The district is also reviewing other programs amid new state laws requiring oversight of AI in schools. Local advocacy groups continue to push for reduced technology use and increased investment in traditional educational resources.

items.title: South Korea's top Certified Tax Accountant exam scorer admits to cheating using AI and hidden micro-camera [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Korea's top tax accountant exam scorer confesses to cheating with AI
items.summary: The highest scorer on South Korea's Certified Tax Accountant exam confessed to cheating by using a hidden micro-camera to photograph exam papers and a generative AI to produce answers, which he then checked on a smartphone. This confession came after the individual achieved a perfect score far above the average of 16,856 test-takers. The cheating was uncovered following suspicions raised in online communities rather than by exam proctors or official monitoring systems. The incident has sparked concerns about the integrity of credentialing exams amid advancing AI technologies and the challenges of detecting such sophisticated cheating methods. The government has responded by increasing surveillance measures at exam centers, but experts warn that cheating methods may continue to evolve beyond current detection capabilities.

items.title: Analysis: Most AI competitive moats serve as growth fuel rather than durable barriers, with context and know-how becoming less defensible [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Most of AI moats are just fuel
items.summary:
The article argues that many traditional competitive advantages in AI, often called moats, primarily function as accelerators for development rather than lasting protections against competition. It suggests that intelligence itself has become a commodity, and that context or know-how, once considered moats, are increasingly shared and integrated into AI models, reducing their defensibility.

The author distinguishes between true moats, which protect a business without ongoing investment, and fuel, which helps a business grow but does not provide lasting protection. Examples like strong brands and licenses are cited as genuine moats, while factors such as capital, technology, and distribution channels are seen as fuel that accelerates progress but does not prevent competitors from entering the market. This perspective challenges common lists of AI moats and emphasizes the evolving nature of competitive advantage in the AI era.

items.title: Vantage V-AI launches 2-bit ternary key-value cache with attention sinks to optimize memory and efficiency in autoregressive AI model inference [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Vantage-V-AI – 2-bit ternary KV-cache with attention sinks
items.summary:
Vantage V-AI is an open-source inference runtime and streaming engine that addresses key-value cache memory explosion in autoregressive models by using a 2-bit packed ternary representation and attention sinks. It supports constant-complexity generation across CPUs, edge devices, and multi-GPU setups, integrating transparently with Hugging Face models without modifying generation loops.

The system quantizes multi-head attention keys and values into ternary states to reduce storage by nearly 8 times compared to FP16, and employs attention sinks to anchor softmax mass and prevent trajectory collapse during long-sequence generation. Benchmarks demonstrate exact token parity between lossless and dynamic FP8 streaming modes and high retrieval coherence across context lengths up to 4,096 tokens.

items.title: Meituan releases LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter AI agent model trained entirely on Chinese hardware without Nvidia GPUs, achieving near top-tier benchmark scores [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Meituan releases a 1.6-trillion-parameter agent model that never touched an Nvidia GPU
items.summary:
Meituan has unveiled LongCat-2.5, a 1.6-trillion-parameter AI agent model designed for autonomous multi-step tasks, particularly coding, trained exclusively on Chinese hardware without using Nvidia GPUs. The model supports text, image, and video inputs and achieves an 88.4 score on Terminal Bench, close to leading Western models like Claude Opus 5. Deployment runs on a cluster of 194 Huawei Ascend chips, highlighting a significant advancement in large-scale AI training within China.

LongCat-2.5 uses a mixture-of-experts architecture activating about 48 billion parameters per token and processes images by converting them into tokens integrated with text inputs. The model was trained with reinforcement learning on real software tasks and includes distilled capabilities from specialized teacher models. Meituan quantizes the model to 4-bit precision for efficient processing on Chinese chips, maintaining accuracy while improving throughput.

The model's weights are available under an MIT license allowing commercial use, and it supports APIs compatible with OpenAI and Anthropic formats. Meituan offers a chat interface and API access with promotional pricing. This release follows Meituan's earlier LongCat-2.0 model and reflects growing competitiveness of Chinese AI hardware and open-weight models against top US counterparts.

items.title: Carnegie Mellon student develops OATs, AI-powered E Ink devices that turn everyday objects into virtual pets to encourage better habits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets
items.summary:
A Carnegie Mellon PhD student created Object Agent Twins (OATs), small E Ink devices that attach to household items like plants, skateboards, and dumbbells, displaying AI avatars with emotions based on sensor data. These virtual pets aim to motivate users to care for their belongings by showing happiness or sadness depending on the object's condition or usage.

OATs use sensors to monitor factors such as moisture, temperature, and motion, and generate expressive sprites via Google Gemini's image service. Users can customize behaviors through a web portal, setting positive and negative triggers for each object. While the devices have limited battery life of three to four days, they have been tested by users for tracking habits, providing warnings, and enhancing interaction with physical items.

The project was presented at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology, sparking discussion about anthropomorphizing AI and its effects on human connection. The creator has not yet decided whether to commercialize OATs, viewing the current version as a proof of concept rather than a finished product.

items.title: Australia's central bank finds AI impacting young workers in software and customer service roles more than older workers since late 2022 [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Australia's central bank finds AI hitting young workers first, especially in software and customer service
items.summary:
Australia's central bank has identified that artificial intelligence adoption is affecting employment among young entry-level workers, particularly in software development and customer service, with job postings and employment rates declining more sharply for those aged 15 to 24 since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022. The analysis focuses on occupations with high AI exposure and notes that older workers in these fields have not experienced similar declines.

The bank cautions that these trends do not establish direct causation from AI alone, as other factors like post-pandemic business cycle shifts and remote work changes may also influence employment patterns. Similar studies from the US and Denmark show mixed impacts, with some declines in junior technical roles but no broad economy-wide job losses, while AI-related job postings and upskilling efforts continue to grow.

items.title: ShadowDiff launches dual-traffic shadow testing and SQL diffing tool for AI-migrated legacy back ends to detect regressions and ensure production readiness [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: ShadowDiff – Shadow testing and SQL diffing for AI-migrated back ends
items.summary:
ShadowDiff is a network proxy and analysis engine designed to support enterprises migrating legacy back ends to AI-refactored cloud-native services. It duplicates live HTTP traffic to both legacy and AI-migrated services, comparing responses and SQL queries to identify subtle regressions such as serialization discrepancies, transaction leaks, and query inefficiencies.

The tool integrates with Envoy Proxy and Istio Service Mesh for traffic mirroring and uses a three-way differential noise cancellation model to filter out non-deterministic differences. It also synthesizes regression tests using Google Gemini and automates GitHub pull requests for fixes, aiming to reduce the risk that currently prevents many enterprises from deploying AI-modernized back ends to production.

items.title: Lawyer upgrades private AI server with eight Nvidia V100 GPUs to run 80% of DeepSeek v4.1 Flash at 4-bit NVFP4 precision, adds 1TB RAM and RTX 3090, fixes crashes caused by faulty PSU [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Lawyer upgrades eight-V100 private AI server to run 80% of DeepSeek v4.1 Flash
items.summary:
A trial lawyer in Columbia, South Carolina, upgraded his private AI server built on eight Nvidia V100 GPUs to run about 80% of DeepSeek v4.1 Flash at 4-bit NVFP4 precision, increasing RAM to 1TB and adding an Nvidia RTX 3090 GPU. The server supports his legal practice with a custom legal harness and improved model fidelity, despite a slight drop in code output speed. The crashes previously affecting the system were traced to a bad power supply unit rather than PCIe issues.

The upgrade involved running most frequently used model experts at higher precision while keeping others at 2-bit precision to fit within GPU memory limits. The lawyer, identified as Nick Mermiges, founder of PLI Labs and proprietarylegal.ai, built the software side with AI assistance and has been refining the system since early 2026. The system now handles multiple requests concurrently and maintains document privacy by keeping data on-premises.

This enhancement allows the AI server to offload more workload from the lawyer, improving operational efficiency while maintaining high fidelity in model outputs. The Nvidia V100 GPUs remain supported by the last compatible driver branch, with the system continuing to evolve to meet the demands of legal AI applications.

items.title: IBM launches Spyre AI Accelerator PCIe card with 32 AI cores, 128GB LPDDR5 memory, and 300+ TOPS performance at 75W for IBM Z and LinuxONE systems [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: IBM Spyre AI Accelerator Card (75W PCIe Card with 128GB of LPDDR5)
items.summary:
IBM introduced the Spyre AI Accelerator, a PCIe add-on card designed to enhance AI inferencing on IBM Z and LinuxONE platforms. The card features 32 AI accelerator cores, 128GB of LPDDR5 memory, and delivers over 300 trillion operations per second (TOPS) while consuming just 75 watts of power.

Manufactured using Samsung's 5 nm process, the Spyre card supports ensembles of up to eight cards, providing up to 1TB of memory and substantial AI compute capacity. It complements the on-chip Telum-II AI accelerator to enable advanced multi-model inferencing for applications like real-time fraud detection and code assistance, supporting on-premises generative AI workloads such as Watsonx Code Assistant while maintaining IBM Z's security and reliability.

IBM also offers the Appliance Control Center for streamlined deployment and management of software appliances on IBM Z and LinuxONE, along with the Spyre Support Appliance for monitoring and diagnosing Spyre cards in real time to optimize performance and proactively handle errors.

items.originalTitle: The Fallout from Jensen’s Downfall
items.summary: Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia follows revelations of multiple affairs, including with a former executive at a major Nvidia customer, leading to board intervention and widespread fallout across industries. The company’s board, initially reluctant to act due to longstanding ties with Huang, was compelled to respond after pressure from Nvidia’s general counsel. Allegations involving a former executive suspected by some U.S. authorities of espionage added complexity to the situation, though recent reports cast doubt on those claims. Despite the controversy, Huang retains significant support within Silicon Valley and among Nvidia employees, with petitions circulating for his reinstatement. Congressional investigations are expected, with Huang agreeing to testify before Thanksgiving. Observers note that Huang’s leadership style involved overriding cautious executives, and his behavior had been underreported due to Nvidia’s complexity and his public persona as an AI pioneer.

items.originalSummary:
Welcome, Weekenders! 

Jexit, as I’d like to christen Huang’s departure from Nvidia, is an ugly matter, an implosion with fallout across continents and several different industries. No one irradiated by it walks away a picture of good health. 

Huang obfuscated the truth, promising senior executives at his company that he’d had just the one affair, with Alice Huang, the former executive at Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. But that wasn’t the case. He reportedly had at least two others, including one with a direct report. 

Nvidia’s board almost didn’t act and only did so on the insistence of the company’s general counsel, Tim Teter. I’m not surprised. The board is dominated by people who’ve known Huang for decades. And there was not even a board chair. 

The friendships Huang thought he had in Washington weren’t nearly enough to save him, a reminder of the fickleness of politics as Silicon Valley goes through the necessary course correction to win influence with the ascendant left. (Alex Karp is a Democrat again, did you hear?) Indeed, it looks pretty obvious that some factions within Trump-led Washington worked against Huang. Many of the reporters who have been most active in the last week are in Washington.

Some U.S. authorities say the former Megaspeed executive was a spy. Was she? More reports in recent days cast doubt on whether she really was. No matter. The mere implication was a useful weapon to wield against Huang. 

The spy-who-loved-him situation was catnip for reporters, but I don’t want to hand out laurels to the media. Huang’s bullying tendencies went underhighlighted for years—first because Nvidia was too complex and confusing to cover, and then because of Huang’s presentation of himself as a nerdish, articulate poster boy for the AI age. It makes me wonder who else is escaping close coverage as the tech landscape continues to widen and morph. 

Throughout Jexit, Huang has maintained a sizable base of support in Silicon Valley. A host of prominent names rushed to his defense—from venture capitalists Vinod Khosla and Ron Conway to Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney. Huang still has a legion of allies within Nvidia. On Thursday evening, a petition from Nvidia employees circulated online advocating for his reinstatement.

I wonder how misguided that hero worship might later seem. Congressional investigations into Huang and Nvidia loom—he has agreed to testify before Thanksgiving—and already we’re starting to see reports about how he really ran Nvidia, a place where he was comfortable steamrolling over more cautious executives. 

Stephen Witt, who wrote a 2025 biography of Huang, “The Thinking Machine,” describes him in a new essay for The New York Times as a person energized “by arrogance and toxic self-regard.” Witt also makes it clear how willfully blind everyone was to Huang’s behavior. When Nvidia began in the early ’90s, its corporate mascot was Dawn, an “underdressed, large-breasted C.G.I. pixie” that was “memory-holed in 2020 around the time Mr. Huang started to talk about empowering women within the company.”

The title of Witt’s book refers to both the technology Huang sold and Huang himself. As Witt has contemplated Jexit, he has mulled whether he might return to covering Huang: “I should write a sequel: ‘The What-Were-You-Thinking?! Machine.’”—Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com)

Listening: “Dropping Names With Brent and Jonny”

Let’s acknowledge the Horta in the room—so to speak. With Patrick Stewart’s death last week, more than a few of us have been feeling nostalgic about “Star Trek,” myself included, and it pushed me toward a welcome discovery: Brent Spiner (aka Data) and Jonathan Frakes (aka Commander Riker) have spent the last few months together debuting a podcast! And it is utterly delightful. 

The conceit behind “Dropping Names With Brent and Jonny” is simple: Guests from across the entertainment firmament join Spiner and Frakes to talk about their careers and how they’ve intersected with other famous people. (A bell dings each time someone drops a name.) It’s a nod to just how far the “Star Trek” acting universe extends, and some of their guests beam in direct from Trek land. William Shatner (Captain Kirk) and LeVar Burton (Chief Engineer Geordi La Forge) have both appeared—as have Michael Dorn (Worf) and Seth MacFarlane (the “Family Guy” creator, who has a major Trek obsession). But the show is not a total Trekkie con: Noah Wyle and Ron Perlman have stopped by, too. 

Another recent guest was Margo Martindale, the beloved character actress (and Frakes’ former Harvard University classmate). I especially enjoyed that conversation. Frequently, “Dropping Names” is a window into B-list Hollywood, an existence beneath the industry’s shiniest tier. It is not an entirely unexplored new world, but it is a strange one filled with what-ifs and missed connections. Stewart escaped from it—Spiner and Frakes never did. Now well into their 70s, both actors seem charmingly comfortable at their place within it.—Abram Brown

Reading: “Ladies’ Man” by Laurence Leamer

A question we’ve all been asking ourselves this week: Why would someone with great wealth and power risk it all for sex?

Well, at least in the case of John F. Kennedy Jr., his lifelong randiness was seemingly an effort to prove to himself that he wasn’t the weak, chronically ill fellow he in fact was. “Sex was an assertion of health—a way to defy his ailments,” Laurence Leamer writes in “Ladies’ Man,” a new biography of JFK told chiefly via his many romances. (Leamer’s 2012 bestseller “Capote’s Women” was turned into FX’s “Feud: Capote vs. the Swans.”) Leamer’s retelling of the president’s life is gossiply enveloping, though it never applies a gimlet-eyed gaze to its handsome, oft-idolized subject. Leamer portrays Kennedy as shallow and callow, with a self-professed “slam, bam, thank-you-ma’am” motto toward women. By Kennedy’s own count, he slept with well over 1,000 women, an estimate he offered casually to a friend without compunction. 

Lovesickness may never have troubled Kennedy, but he did suffer from a number of other ailments, including his famous bad back, as well as Addison’s disease, which affects the adrenal glands. In accounting these maladies, “Ladies’ Man” doubles as an unsettling look at midcentury medicine: Among many procedures and treatments, Kennedy underwent four back surgeries and relied on small, steroid-filled pellets inserted under his skin. As Leamer dryly notes in an observation as true of the Kennedys’ era as of our own, “the wealthy sometimes pursue experimental cures that most other people would never consider.”

“Ladies’ Man” broadly charts the Kennedy clan’s rise to prominence, an ascendance marked by the dalliances of JFK’s sister Kathleen, a London socialite who later attached herself to “one of the great roués” of British nobility, and those of his millionaire father. The paterfamilias had his own bravado thinking on fornication—“I want to get the most out of life, including sex”—and was known to labor over hiring a new secretary, sometimes interviewing several dozen applicants.

In several chapters, Leamer shows the extent to which elites like the Kennedys will go to keep their misdeeds hidden. That was never more important to JFK than it became in cloaking his affair with Marilyn Monroe. When gossip spread about the president’s relationship with the actress, Kennedy coerced friend William Haddad, a former journalist turned Peace Corps inspector general, to dispel the rumors among the media even though they were true. “He lied to me,” Haddad recalled. “He used my credibility.”—A.B.

Watching: “Primetime”

The film from director Lance Oppenheim that has lately sucked up so much of the oxygen within pop culture is his joint production with Nathan Fielder—yes, that would be “You Can See Everything,” the Elizabeth Holmes documentary. Perhaps I could also direct your attention to the other Oppenheim movie that came out this fall, “Primetime,” which is newly available for streaming rental. 

Like “You Can See Everything,” “Primetime” is a movie about complicated deceptions, exploitation and false identities—a fictionalized biopic of NBC journalist Chris Hansen, host of “To Catch a Predator,” the short-lived, hidden-camera show from the 2000s that set up sting operations to capture men who wanted child sex. Hansen is portrayed by Robert Pattinson, who brings a reptilian carnivorousness to a star turn that will probably nab him an Oscar nomination. The supporting performances are also excellent, with Emmy winner Merritt Wever as “To Catch a Predator” producer Andie Bender and Skyler Gisondo as Decoy Dan, a youthful, almost androgynous actor who assumes the role of onscreen bait. 

Oppenheim keeps “Primetime”’s focus narrow, and it unfolds over the first few months of Hansen’s frantic campaign to turn his ickfest into a hit NBC program that could compete against ABC’s “Lost.” Oppenheim’s camerawork and shot selection in “Primetime” feels like a somewhat unfamiliar style for a feature film—a reflection of his decade-plus career in documentaries. (His “Ren Faire,” which examined the drama around a Renaissance fair in Texas, was a 2024 HBO standout.) Oppenheim likes shadows and grimy soft focus, and what he ends up with is a vérité-esque haunted house picture. (The climax comes as a fierce rainstorm lashes a tidy suburban home, calling to mind “Poltergeist”’s finale.) The most obvious ghouls in “Primetime” are the sex perverts, who are summoned and duly exorcised in quick order. They’re not the only dark souls, though: Hansen is another, scheming to seize fame and snare increasingly prominent men on camera. And thus emerges a further thematic link between “Primetime” and “You Can See Everything”: Both feature protagonists wearing masks of attractive ambition over their monstrous tendencies. Still, it’s sparse camouflage.—A.B.

items.title: Anthropic CEO Amodei acknowledges major uncertainty over next year’s outcomes days before planned record $64.4 billion IPO [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic CEO Amodei admits "there's a huge uncertainty in what's going to happen next year" days before a record IPO
items.summary:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei highlighted significant uncertainty about the company's future just days before its planned IPO, which aims to raise up to $64.4 billion. He described purchasing compute capacity as the company's biggest business challenge, noting that commitments have reached nearly $901 billion, mostly tied to compute and chips, with $71 billion due by September 2027. The IPO is intended to provide a financial buffer against the risks of mismatched spending and revenue.

Amodei explained that compute must be bought one to two years in advance, before revenue potential is clear, creating a risk of over- or under-investment. To mitigate this, Anthropic maintains strong gross margins, a large cash balance, and uses the spot market for additional compute capacity as needed. The company’s annualized revenue run rate reached $81 billion by October 2026, driven by growing demand for its AI products. Amodei also expressed cautious optimism about AI’s potential to address major diseases within 5 to 15 years.

items.originalTitle: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn’t make it
items.summary:
Several high-profile AI projects and startups have shut down or failed to meet expectations, illustrating the challenges in the AI industry. Notable examples include Character.ai, which filed for bankruptcy after legal and operational difficulties, and Apple's Siri AI, which faced repeated delays before its recent rollout. OpenAI also experienced setbacks with its ChatGPT redesign and discontinued standalone apps like ChatGPT Atlas and Sora.

According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, about 42% of corporate AI initiatives are eventually abandoned due to funding, technical, or market challenges. Other projects like Relay, an AI workflow automation tool, and privacy-focused assistant Ollie also ceased operations amid competition and scaling difficulties. This growing "AI graveyard" highlights the risks and lessons for companies investing in AI development.

items.title: Anthropic says outdated prompting habits slow Claude Opus 5.5 and recommends new usage guidelines for improved performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic says outdated prompting habits are slowing down Claude Opus 5.5
items.summary:
Anthropic has made Claude Opus 5.5 the default model on all paid plans and advises users to abandon prompting phrases like "think hard" that date back to older models, as these slow down response times without improving quality. The company recommends starting at the "Medium" effort level, which matches the previous model's "High" setting, and adjusting only if necessary to optimize cost and performance.

Anthropic also suggests describing desired outcomes in a single message rather than step-by-step instructions, attaching diagrams as images instead of typing them out, and specifying unwanted design styles explicitly rather than using vague bans. The model's improved capabilities allow it to handle multi-part tasks and image reading more effectively, reducing the need for manual intervention and enabling faster, more accurate results.

items.title: Helen Toner, former OpenAI board member who voted to fire Sam Altman, warns against trusting AI CEOs for safety oversight [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
items.summary:
Helen Toner, executive director of Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology and former OpenAI board member involved in the decision to fire Sam Altman, discusses the challenges of AI safety governance. She argues that relying on any single AI CEO to ensure safe development is risky, especially as commercial pressures conflict with safety commitments.

Toner highlights the failure of OpenAI's nonprofit board to enforce its mission during the leadership crisis known as "the blip," which led to Altman's reinstatement and a board restructuring. She also addresses broader AI safety concerns, including recent AI model breaches and the limitations of voluntary regulatory accords, emphasizing the need for smarter AI regulation and accountability mechanisms beyond individual trust.

items.originalTitle: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
items.summary:
Ransomware attacks have surged in 2026, with researchers noting a 20 to 40 percent increase in alleged incidents over the summer compared to spring. Cybercriminals are increasingly using AI tools to enhance phishing, negotiation, and other attack phases, enabling less experienced actors to launch ransomware operations independently.

While fully automated AI ransomware has not yet appeared, experts observe that AI is accelerating the growth and fragmentation of ransomware groups globally, particularly outside the United States. Some new groups have rapidly claimed dozens of victims, raising concerns about the evolving threat landscape and the potential for further AI-driven automation in cybercrime.

items.title: Study finds AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity frequently recommend scam or counterfeit shopping websites, with Perplexity showing risky sites in 15% of responses [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Chatbots Won’t Stop Recommending Scam Websites to People Trying to Shop
items.summary:
A study by Podqi reported by The Verge found that leading AI chatbots often suggest fraudulent or knockoff retail websites when users ask about shopping options for various brands. Perplexity recommended risky sites in 15% of answers, ChatGPT in 8%, and Gemini in 4%, with many recommendations lacking warnings about potential scams.

The chatbots were tested using questions about top websites, international shipping, and regional sites for 151 brands, including major names like Lululemon and Birkenstock. Smaller brands were more likely to be replaced by scam sites in responses, and certain queries triggered more dubious suggestions. Although ChatGPT sometimes warned users, most risky site recommendations were presented without caution.

Experts warn consumers to verify sources before providing personal or payment information, as AI chatbots present answers as definitive despite being vulnerable to manipulation. This issue highlights ongoing challenges in distinguishing trustworthy content online amid increasing AI adoption for internet searches and shopping.

items.title: FAA introduces AI-powered SMART air traffic control amid pilotless flight milestones and industry concerns over safety and reliability [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: No Pilots. Few Air Traffic Controllers. What Could Go Wrong?
items.summary:
The FAA has launched SMART, an AI-infused air traffic management system aimed at reducing delays and improving efficiency, coinciding with a national groundstop that disrupted airline schedules. Meanwhile, Joby Aviation completed a 3,200-mile pilotless flight across the US, marking a significant step in autonomous aviation technology.

These developments reflect a rapid AI integration into the traditionally cautious aviation sector, which has been preparing for robotic aircraft and drones since the early 2000s through initiatives like the NextGen air transportation system. Despite technological advances and commercial interest from companies like Amazon, Walmart, and Google, industry insiders express concerns about the safety and reliability of these new AI systems.

The ongoing AI revolution in aviation promises to transform air travel economics and operations, but questions remain about trust and regulatory readiness as the sector balances innovation with safety.

items.title: OpenAI disbands robotics team, reallocates researchers as GPT-6 Astra general-purpose model shows strong robotics control capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI reassigns robotics researchers to other teams as general-purpose models might make specialized robotics AI unnecessary
items.summary:
OpenAI is dissolving its standalone robotics team and reassigning researchers to other groups, citing advances in general-purpose models like GPT-6 Astra that can directly control robots and reduce the need for specialized robotics AI. The company aims to accelerate robotics development by integrating robotics expertise into broader AI research teams.

Tests show GPT-6 Astra outperforming specialized robotics models in simulated tasks, achieving higher success rates and better task completion scores. Despite these advances, it remains unclear how much robotics-specific data was used in training, and specialized models may still offer benefits in cost, reliability, and efficiency. OpenAI plans a public robot demo by 2027 but faces financial pressures to focus on core AI products amid competition from other AI firms.

items.title: Google Cloud makes Compute Engine API multi-versioning generally available with immutable quarterly date-based versions starting 2026-09-01
items.originalTitle: Google Cloud Moves the Compute Engine API to Immutable Date-Based Versions
items.summary:
Google Cloud has introduced immutable, date-stamped versions of its Compute Engine API, replacing the single mutable /v1 endpoint with quarterly snapshots named by date, such as 2026-09-01. Callers select versions via a header or query parameter, allowing new versions to change defaults, error formats, and IAM checks without affecting existing /v1 users. This approach aligns with Google's API Improvement Proposals and follows models used by Azure Resource Manager and Stripe.

The new versioning enables safer configuration defaults and tighter permission checks while maintaining backward compatibility for existing clients. Client libraries for multiple languages now bind to specific date-based versions without changing import paths, and tools like gcloud and Terraform have been updated to support the new scheme. Google has not announced an end-of-life date for /v1 or plans to extend this versioning to other Google Cloud APIs.

On dating apps, some users explicitly reject AI use or AI professionals as potential partners, citing concerns about societal impacts and future uncertainties. Meanwhile, others employ AI tools to manage their dating lives, illustrating the city's complex relationship with the technology. This shift highlights a broader cultural tension in the region between embracing AI innovation and addressing its social consequences.

items.originalTitle: Jensen Didn’t Create the AI Boom. It Created Him.
items.summary:
If you follow investors and reporters on X, you would get the sense that the resignation of Jensen Huang amounts to the end of the AI boom. A summary of my X feed Wednesday morning would go something like “I hope the Nvidia board knew what they were doing before ending the world as we know it.”

But if you believe that to be true, you haven’t been paying attention. Because as much as Jensen created the AI boom (and clearly Nvidia’s GPU—the brains that trains AI models—did), the AI boom created Jensen. And that’s key to understanding the world that comes after his reign.

items.title: Where companies should place their AI bets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where companies should place their AI bets
items.summary:
After several years of pushing organizationwide AI adoption, companies are now confronting the cost. As boardroom conversations shift to return on investment, business leaders are taking a harder look at which AI bets to fund and scale.

To understand what questions executives should be asking ahead of AI investments, Meredith Mazzilli, The Information’s finance editor, spoke with three experts approaching AI from different perspectives.

  • Karen Young, chair of the U.S. board of partners and U.S. sales leader, PwC
  • Mimi Carsley, chief financial officer and treasurer, Jack Henry & Associates
  • Heidi Rhodes, global director, enterprise GTM customer success and sales enablement, Meta Platforms

Resetting Priorities

At Meta Platforms, Mark Zuckerberg has taken an experimentation-first approach, making AI adoption a priority across the company.

“He basically said, ‘This is going to be the year that everyone is going to adopt AI.’ We told our employees, ‘Figure out what works and go fail,’” recalled Heidi Rhodes.

That freedom to experiment helped Meta identify which workflows benefited from AI and standardize around them. Initially, token consumption wasn’t a concern, a luxury Rhodes acknowledged not every organization can afford.

“In 2023, it was: Any single problem that you have, rub some AI on it. Then we got our token bills,” she said. “Now organizations are saying, ‘Unless you can show me real ROI, we can end the conversation there.’”

Other companies took a more cautious route. Jack Henry & Associates, which operates in the highly regulated financial services industry, started with governance, establishing guardrails for assessing and approving AI tools and determining what data employees could access, said CFO Mimi Carsley.

At PwC, the challenge is less a shortage of ideas than deciding which ones are worth pursuing. Employees across PwC are embracing AI and exploring new ways to integrate it into their work. Karen Young said the deciding factor in funding ideas remains the client, much as it did before AI.

“We think about the solutions our clients are looking for and how we can scale [our AI tools] for their benefit,” she said.

Controlling Spend

At Jack Henry, providing Microsoft Copilot licenses to all 7,300 associates could add $3 million in costs, said Carsley. The company therefore regularly reassesses who needs access.

“If someone’s not using their license, we’ll go talk to them and coach them up. If they’re still not using it, we actually seize it back and redeploy it elsewhere in the organization,” she said.

Young said PwC has also shifted to training employees to be more efficient with their usage.

“We lead them to use the right tool for the right model for the right reason,” she said.

Measuring What Matters

One way organizations can prioritize AI spending is to look beyond efficiency gains to how those gains are put to use. By way of example, Young cited a client that transformed 14 finance processes, cutting forecasting and scenario planning from weeks to minutes.

“The real question is: What are those employees in finance now doing to be more strategic with their time?” she asked.

Carsley said companies also need to consider how they are using those time savings and whether they can redeploy investment elsewhere.

“If someone’s gonna use AI to draft an email and you save five minutes, like, did you go get a cup of coffee or did you do something with the five minutes?” she said. “If you’re not redeploying that savings to another productivity or efficiency, did you really gain anything by the spend?”

Rhodes, meanwhile, cautioned against treating efficiency gains as an excuse to reduce headcount. She cited a client whose sales team became 20% to 30% more productive after AI took over hours of research.

“Do you make a reduction in humans? Or now that you have one of the world’s most efficient salespeople, do you go out and hire more?” she asked, adding that her vote is for the latter.

Ultimately, though, AI prioritization comes down to a company’s unique advantage.

“Ask yourself, what do you have an advantage in? Then apply AI to that as an accelerant,” advised Carsley. “Do the thing you do best as an organization, then turn it up 10% to 20%.”

Other companies took a more cautious route. Jack Henry & Associates, which operates in the highly regulated financial services industry, started with governance, establishing guardrails for assessing and approving AI tools and determining what data employees could access, said CFO Mimi Carsley.

At PwC, the challenge is less a shortage of ideas than deciding which ones are worth pursuing. Employees across PwC are embracing AI and exploring new ways to integrate it into their work. Karen Young said the deciding factor in funding ideas remains the client, much as it did before AI.

“We think about the solutions our clients are looking for and how we can scale [our AI tools] for their benefit,” she said.

Controlling Spend

At Jack Henry, providing Microsoft Copilot licenses to all 7,300 associates could add $3 million in costs, said Carsley. The company therefore regularly reassesses who needs access.

“If someone’s not using their license, we’ll go talk to them and coach them up. If they’re still not using it, we actually seize it back and redeploy it elsewhere in the organization,” she said.

Young said PwC has also shifted to training employees to be more efficient with their usage.

“We lead them to use the right tool for the right model for the right reason,” she said.

Measuring What Matters

One way organizations can prioritize AI spending is to look beyond efficiency gains to how those gains are put to use. By way of example, Young cited a client that transformed 14 finance processes, cutting forecasting and scenario planning from weeks to minutes.

“The real question is: What are those employees in finance now doing to be more strategic with their time?” she asked.

Carsley said companies also need to consider how they are using those time savings and whether they can redeploy investment elsewhere.

“If someone’s gonna use AI to draft an email and you save five minutes, like, did you go get a cup of coffee or did you do something with the five minutes?” she said. “If you’re not redeploying that savings to another productivity or efficiency, did you really gain anything by the spend?”

Rhodes, meanwhile, cautioned against treating efficiency gains as an excuse to reduce headcount. She cited a client whose sales team became 20% to 30% more productive after AI took over hours of research.

“Do you make a reduction in humans? Or now that you have one of the world’s most efficient salespeople, do you go out and hire more?” she asked, adding that her vote is for the latter.

Ultimately, though, AI prioritization comes down to a company’s unique advantage.

“Ask yourself, what do you have an advantage in? Then apply AI to that as an accelerant,” advised Carsley. “Do the thing you do best as an organization, then turn it up 10% to 20%.”

items.title: Sex, Lies and AI Chips: Jensen Huang’s Last Days as Nvidia CEO
items.originalTitle: Sex, Lies and AI Chips: Jensen Huang’s Last Days as Nvidia CEO
items.summary:
Last weekend, all hell broke loose around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

On Friday, his intimate relationship with a suspected Chinese spy was made public. Then Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, came to Huang’s home and asked him whether a news report about the relationship was true, according to a person briefed on the interaction. Huang told him it was. By Sunday evening, Huang had publicly apologized for the affair, and Nvidia’s board had said it would investigate his conduct. Teter had to urge directors to do so—the board, which includes executives who’ve known Huang for decades, had been reluctant to act.

In conversations with senior Nvidia executives, Huang maintained that the affair with the woman, Alice Huang, was his only infidelity, according to people familiar with the situation. Had that been the case, perhaps he would have made it through the maelstrom.

items.title: How Much Is Anthropic Really Worth? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Much Is Anthropic Really Worth?
items.summary:
While investors digest the news of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang’s exit and its implications on the AI build-out, they are simultaneously mulling another nebulous question: How much is Anthropic worth?

If everything goes according to plan, the market should give its answer when the company debuts on the Nasdaq exchange next week. Anthropic has set a tentative pricing range of between $1.25 trillion and $1.4 trillion, but several investors we spoke to expect it to price above that range. 

Pricing an initial public offering above the proposed range “is a signal of underlying demand momentum, which is very important to get people excited to participate,” said Samantha Lau, chief investment officer of small- and mid-cap growth equities at AllianceBernstein.
